next_changelog: [When to Segment]: added permissive rules to split at internal sentence-final punctuation (?/./!) that closes a complete clause, after quoted/embedded questions ending in '?' before their reporting clause, and after -거든/-는데 when the following clause introduces its own new subject/topic as an independent elaboration — fixes measured under-segmentation cases.

[Never Segment]: replaced sweeping caution with precise, condition-based bans — do not split a causal/result connective when the following span is a fragment lacking a finite verb, do not split inside a clause containing 3+ filler/self-correction repetitions (since no boundary there helps), and do not multiply splits across a short sequential-action chain (under ~15 words) joined by repeated -고 connectives — targets the measured over-segmentation and wrong-boundary cases without banning any connective ending outright.

next_changelog: [When to Segment]: added explicit permissive rules to split before a discourse marker (그런데, 근데, 그래서, 그러니까) that begins a new clause even when the preceding clause ends in a causal/result connective or the discourse-marker clause trails off without a finished predicate, and reinforced that internal sentence-final punctuation (?/./!) is always a safe split point regardless of whether following material still elaborates the same referent — recovers the measured under-segmentation cases (그런데/그래서/? left unsplit) at no quality cost.

[Never Segment]: narrowed the causal/result-connective-fragment ban so it no longer blocks splits when the trailing span is itself introduced by a discourse marker (그래서/그러니까/근데/그런데), and removed the overly broad 'trailing ? on bare NP' prohibition since it was suppressing safe, measured latency gains at real punctuation boundaries — direction says segment more aggressively, so over-broad prohibitions are narrowed/removed rather than adding new restrictions.

next_changelog: [Core Principles]: Added an explicit statement that because measured quality sits far above the floor, the default action at any completed clause-final connective/ender is to split; withholding a split now requires a concrete, nameable piece of information that would be lost, not generic caution about disfluency, density, or list structure — this pushes latency gain up without adding any new prohibition.

[Decision Procedure]: Reworded steps 5-6 so that only a specific, nameable loss of information (a word, referent, tense, or polarity that cannot be recovered) blocks a split; vague unease about a sentence being 'dense', 'disfluent', or part of a 'list/chain' no longer counts as sufficient grounds to withhold a <SEG> — this narrows how conservatively the existing checklist is applied, directly increasing segmentation frequency as the critic's 'segment more aggressively' direction requires, without touching [When to Segment] or [Never Segment], which were changed (and reverted) in the immediately preceding iteration.
